extracted.intended_audience: Presbyterian ministers, church officers, historians and readers interested in ecclesiastical polity and the Revolution settlement of religion (late 17th–early 18th century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate the legitimacy, lawfulness, and faithfulness of the Revolution-era settlement of religion (esp. 1689–1716) from a Presbyterian/theological perspective, focusing on church-state relations, authority, discipline, and ministerial qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil magistrate must not assume administration of the word or the keys
rubrics_metrics.description: "The civil magistrate may not assume to himself the administration of the word or the keys." (Confession of Faith, chap. xxiii, sect. 3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites scripture and the Confession of Faith to assert that ecclesiastical authority (preaching, governance, the power of the keys) belongs to church officers, not to civil rulers. Examples of breach: royal/parliamentary interference in convocating assemblies or determining church discipline. Anti-pattern: magistrates issuing directions that effectively control church teaching or discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church officers are the primary bearers of church power
rubrics_metrics.description: All power of church matters, whether respecting doctrine or government, has been committed by Christ to church officers as the first, proper receptacles thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper order for reformation: the church goes first in reform and the state should follow by ratification and defense of the church's acts. Civil rulers making alterations in church government by their own authority is characterized as usurpation and tyrannical encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: No civil licence required for church convocation or judicatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that make it unlawful for the church to convocate its superior judicatories except by the king's licence are an invasion on Christ's headship and the church's intrinsic power (e.g., Act 1592 and its revival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revival/renewal of such clauses (as in the Revolution settlement) is judged Erastian. The text points to provisions that require royal/parliamentary indictment or licence for assemblies and treats such requirements as stripping the church of constitutionality and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assemblies and church constitutions must not be subordinate to sovereign/parliamentary authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal commissions that presuppose assemblies exist 'by our decree' indicate the assembly's power and right of constitution are regarded as subordinate to the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instances cited: assemblies being called, adjourned, prorogued, or dissolved by royal authority (1691–1694 examples), restrictions on membership and matters to be discussed, and the practice of requiring oaths by law to exclude members. Such interference is evidence of Erastian practice and invalidates ecclesiastical independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlements of church government must be founded on Scripture and divine right, not popular inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate settlement should be 'built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets' and on scriptural warrant, not merely 'agreeable to the inclinations of the people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticizes the Revolution acts for abolishing Prelacy and establishing Presbytery on grounds of antiquity or popular inclination rather than scriptural proof; treating multiple, inconsistent forms (Presbytery in Scotland, Prelacy in England) as both 'agreeable to God's word' is self-contradictory and indicates a latitudinarian, political settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church must formally and explicitly condemn Erastian encroachments
rubrics_metrics.description: If the church does not expressly condemn Erastianism and assert Christ's sole headship, its silence or acquiescence is construed as consent to civil supremacy over ecclesiastical affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reproves assemblies for failing to pass explicit acts condemning Erastianism (e.g., not formally asserting the alone headship of Christ), and notes that omission of explanatory acts when requiring subscription to the Confession evidences compliance with civil impositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil authorities must not forbid or obstruct ecclesiastical discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil imposition that forbids church judicatories from exercising discipline (for example, protecting episcopal curates from church process) is an unlawful interference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include royal letters instructing assemblies to make 'no distinction' and to receive ministers who formerly conformed to Episcopacy, and parliamentary acts protecting such curates in their benefices while restricting church discipline. Anti-pattern: civil authorities stopping church processes or preventing removal of scandalous clergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reception of former episcopal clergy must require repentance and renunciation of prelacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Receiving former episcopal ministers on merely an acknowledgement of the civil settlement (without renouncing prelacy or showing repentance) is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Assembly's 'sham formula' (1694) for receiving curates—omitting any renunciation of prelacy or requirement of repentance—is criticized as allowing scandalous persons in without moral or doctrinal reformation. Proper practice requires evidence of contrition and conformity to church government and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministerial qualifications must be determined by Christ's Word and church judicatory, not by civil statute or oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: It pertains to Christ to appoint qualifications of his officers in the Word, and to church representatives to declare who is qualified for ministry; civil statutes prescribing oaths and qualifications are usurpations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts cited (1693, 1695, etc.) requiring oaths of allegiance/assurance, uniformity of worship, and deprivation ipso facto for non-compliance are presented as civil impositions that substitute parliamentary requirements for scriptural ministerial qualifications. Anti-pattern: ministers deprived by civil statute rather than church judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil magistrate must not prescribe worship forms or impose liturgical texts under ecclesiastical pains
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary acts that demand uniformity of worship, specify prayers (e.g., prayer for the monarch in express words), or require reading of civil acts in church under ecclesiastical penalties profane the Lord's day and corrupt worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: acts commanding monthly fasts with fines and processes for ministers; act of 1737 requiring reading of a statute in parish churches with ecclesiastical penalties for neglect. The page treats such civil impositions as profaning divine worship and a further example of Erastianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of public fasts and thanksgivings belongs to the church, not the civil magistrate
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to appoint solemn fasts and thanksgivings is entrusted to spiritual office-bearers; kings/parliaments appointing national fasts with civil pains is an encroachment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptural references (Joel, Jeremiah, Numbers, Matthew) are used to argue that fasting/solemnities are ecclesiastical functions. The practice of the state appointing monthly fasts (with fines and reports to privy council) and the church's compliance are criticized, especially when such fasts were for wars with Catholic powers (seen as contrary to Protestant/Presbyterian principles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil imposition of ecclesiastical pains for nonconformity to civil statutes is unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts that impose ecclesiastical penalties (disabling ministers from sitting/voting in judicatories, depriving them of benefices) for failing to obey civil directives are illegitimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fines and ecclesiastical disabilities for not observing state-appointed fasts; penalties for not reading prescribed acts in church. The page argues these acts effectively subject spiritual office to civil discipline and punishments, contrary to the church's autonomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of civilly-imposed oaths that supersede covenantal or scriptural commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Oaths of allegiance/assurance/abjuration imposed by parliament (and enforced under pain) that replace the oaths of covenant or bind ministers to civil polity are improper qualifications for ecclesiastical office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts requiring such oaths as sine qua non for ministers, university principals, and for admission to preach are cited (1693, 1706, 1707, early George I acts). The page condemns replacing covenantal oaths with parliamentary ones and making compliance a condition of ministry under threat of deprivation or banishment.
